advisory.checklist_item: - [ ] Distinguish a scan TIMEOUT (do not advance the cursor — leave state byte-identical so the next run recovers the interval) from a genuinely rotated-past cursor (reseed) in the rc!=0 branch of journal_marker_delta.
evidence: observability.sh:460-471: `rc=$?` then `if [ "$rc" -ne 0 ]; then ... journal_tail_cursor "$@" || return 1; [ -n "$JOURNAL_TAIL_CURSOR" ] && journal_state_write "$state_file" "$prev_total" "$JOURNAL_TAIL_CURSOR"`
The rc!=0 branch cannot distinguish timeout (124) from cursor-rotated-past; both reseed the cursor to the tail
Ticket AC5: 'Such a scan leaves the counter's persisted state byte-identical' — a timeout here does NOT leave state byte-identical, it advances the cursor

Test test_unmeasurable_journal_publishes_nothing_and_keeps_its_state (test_observability_journal_bounding_1205.py:302) stubs journalctl to `exit 1` UNCONDITIONALLY, so the tail reseed read also fails and `journal_tail_cursor "$@" || return 1` returns before writing state — the timeout-then-readable-tail path (state DOES change) is never exercised
advisory.finding: A timed-out `--after-cursor` scan (timeout exit 124) is treated identically to a journald-rotated-past cursor: the rc!=0 branch reseeds the cursor from the tail, advancing it past every unread entry. When the scan is merely slow-but-readable (cold cache with a large backlog after the cursor — the exact original outage condition), the tail read `-n 1` succeeds fast and the cursor is moved forward, so all markers between the old cursor and the tail are permanently dropped and never counted in any interval.
scenarios: Cold page cache with a large backlog of entries after the persisted cursor causes the --after-cursor scan to exceed JOURNAL_SCAN_TIMEOUT while the journal itself remains readable — real error markers accumulated during the slow interval are skipped permanently
advisory.suggested_fix: Capture the `bounded`/timeout exit status distinctly: when rc==124 (timeout) do NOT reseed — leave both total and cursor untouched and return 1 so the interval is retried; only reseed from the tail when the read fails for a non-timeout reason (cursor rejected). Add a test that stubs journalctl to time out on --after-cursor but answer -n 1 quickly, asserting the cursor is unchanged.

advisory.checklist_item: - [ ] Bound the debris `du` walk with its own named timeout (e.g. a DEBRIS_DU_TIMEOUT) rather than reusing JOURNAL_SCAN_TIMEOUT.
evidence: observability.sh:715: `entry_kb=$(bounded "$JOURNAL_SCAN_TIMEOUT" du -sk "$entry" ...)`
observability.sh:371-373: `mechanism-ok: env_var JOURNAL_SCAN_TIMEOUT ... the §2d wall-clock bound on every journald read` — the name and doc scope it to journald reads, not a du walk
advisory.finding: The data-disk debris `du` walk is bounded with `JOURNAL_SCAN_TIMEOUT`, a variable named and documented as the per-journal-scan wall-clock bound. A filesystem stat-walk and a journalctl read are unrelated operations; coupling them means any future retuning of the journal-scan timeout silently changes the debris-walk bound (and vice versa), and the name misdescribes what it bounds at this call site.
scenarios: A future change tunes JOURNAL_SCAN_TIMEOUT for journal-read performance and unintentionally changes the debris-walk bound
advisory.suggested_fix: Introduce a distinct timeout variable for the debris du walk (mirroring DOCKER_DU_TIMEOUT/DOCKER_DF_TIMEOUT) so its bound is independent of the journal-scan bound.

advisory.checklist_item: - [ ] Handle the rc!=0 + empty-tail-cursor case so an invalid cursor over a currently-empty journal is cleared (or seeded empty) rather than left stale and stalling the counter.
evidence: observability.sh:468-470: `journal_tail_cursor "$@" || return 1` then `[ -n "$JOURNAL_TAIL_CURSOR" ] && journal_state_write ...` — when the tail read returns rc=0 with an empty cursor, no reseed occurs and the invalid cursor is left in place
Comment at :464 claims 'an entry journald no longer holds cannot stall the counter forever', but an empty journal with an invalid stored cursor does stall it
advisory.finding: In the rc!=0 reseed branch, if the journal is genuinely empty (tail read succeeds with rc=0 but yields an empty cursor), `[ -n "$JOURNAL_TAIL_CURSOR" ]` is false so no state is written and the stale invalid cursor persists. If the original cursor was invalid (rotated past) and the journal is now empty, every subsequent run repeats the failed --after-cursor read and the counter stalls, never publishing again until entries reappear.
scenarios: A counter's cursor is rotated past AND the target journal (e.g. a container that was removed) is currently empty — the counter repeats the failing after-cursor read every interval and never self-heals until entries reappear

advisory.checklist_item: - [ ] Add a test that runs the probe with no `timeout` on PATH and asserts new markers are still counted/published via the `bounded()` direct-run fallback.
evidence: Added code: `if command -v timeout >/dev/null 2>&1; then bounded() { timeout "$@"; } else bounded() { shift; "$@"; } fi`

Named violating input: run the probe on a host with no `timeout` on PATH over a journal containing new AUTODEPLOY_MCP_RETIRE_CAP markers — the fallback must still count and publish them; no test removes `timeout` from the stubbed PATH.
search_files over tests/scripts shows every observability_* test calls `_stub(bin_dir, "timeout", ...)`; none exercise the missing-timeout case.
advisory.finding: The newly added `timeout`-absent degradation branch of `bounded()` (`else bounded() { shift; "$@"; }`) is never exercised: every observability test unconditionally installs a `timeout` stub on PATH, so only the `timeout`-present branch runs. The fallback silently drops the seconds argument and runs the command directly; a mis-shift would mis-invoke every bounded journalctl/du/git call and go undetected.
advisory.suggested_fix: Add a case in test_observability_journal_bounding_1205.py that omits the `timeout` stub (or points PATH at a bin dir without it) and asserts a non-zero delta is still published for a journal with new markers, confirming the `shift; "$@"` fallback invokes journalctl correctly.

advisory.checklist_item: - [ ] Bound the total debris-scan wall time (or cap the number of entries walked), not just each individual du, so the debris loop fits the nested timeout budget.
evidence: infra/scripts/observability.sh:703 `for entry in "$DATA_MOUNT"/* "$DATA_MOUNT"/.[!.]*; do`
infra/scripts/observability.sh:715 `entry_kb=$(bounded "$JOURNAL_SCAN_TIMEOUT" du -sk "$entry" ...)`

infra/scripts/observability.sh:368 `The scan is wall-clock bounded as well, and the bounds NEST: 12 scans x 10 s = 120 s < the 240 s TimeoutStartSec` — the per-entry debris du loop is not included in this count
advisory.finding: The debris `du` walk bounds each entry individually with `bounded "$JOURNAL_SCAN_TIMEOUT"` (10s) inside a loop over an unbounded number of data-mount entries, so aggregate wall-clock is N*10s and is not accounted for in the 12*10s=120s nesting budget; a data mount with many debris directories could exceed the 240s TimeoutStartSec and be SIGKILLed mid-run.

advisory.checklist_item: - [ ] Document/enforce that the production host always has coreutils `timeout`, or provide a non-timeout wall-clock guard for the debris du walk when `timeout` is unavailable.
evidence: infra/scripts/observability.sh:383-385 `else` / `bounded() { shift; "$@"; }`
infra/scripts/observability.sh:713-715 debris `du` walks `whatever happens to be on the data mount` via `bounded`
commit message: "`bounded` degrades to running the command directly where coreutils `timeout` is absent"
advisory.finding: When coreutils `timeout` is absent, `bounded` degrades to running the command directly, which for the debris `du -sk` walk over arbitrary-size directories reintroduces exactly the unbounded-external-command defect class this change claims to close for the sibling sweep.

evidence: install-observability.sh:41 `TimeoutStartSec=240` with no TimeoutStopSec/KillMode set in the [Service] block (lines 27-46)
rebar-autodeploy.service:40 `TimeoutStartSec=90` with no TimeoutStopSec/KillMode
ABSENCE: no `TimeoutStopSec=` or `KillMode=` in either rendered [Service] section
advisory.finding: Both units now depend on systemd SIGKILL (TimeoutStartSec) to bound a hung run, but neither sets TimeoutStopSec or KillMode. Under the exact incident condition (IOPS-saturated volume), a `du`/journalctl child stuck in uninterruptible-sleep (D state) will not respond to SIGKILL promptly, so the run may persist past the intended 240s/90s bound and continue delaying the timer's re-arm.

evidence: infra/scripts/install-observability.sh:45-46: `Nice=10` / `IOSchedulingClass=idle`
infra/systemd/rebar-autodeploy.service:41-42: `Nice=10` / `IOSchedulingClass=idle`
ABSENCE: no verification that the root/data block devices use a scheduler (CFQ/BFQ) that honors IOSchedulingClass=idle; modern NVMe/gp3 defaults (mq-deadline/none) ignore ioprio idle class
dropped.finding: IOSchedulingClass=idle only takes effect under CFQ/BFQ I/O schedulers; on NVMe/gp3 volumes commonly using mq-deadline or none, the idle I/O class is silently ignored, so the I/O-priority throttling intended to prevent the IOPS-saturation outage may not actually engage on the deployment host.
